chapter_theme: A single song at Thiruvanchiyam (திருவாஞ்சியம்) on kings: lords of elephant armies and conquered directions, perfumed and jewelled, end as a handful of ash when the life slips away, yet they do not think to worship Murugan's feet; the praise names Vishnu of Venkatam and Murugan as Kama's kin.

812.reading: The poet describes kings: lords of elephants and the wheel of rule, commanding armies, honoured, conquering the directions, swelling with pride on round cushions, with victory garlands, silks, perfumes and jewels, whose body, when the life slips away among the kin, is lit with fire and becomes a handful of ash; they do not know it, and with longing do not think to worship Murugan's feet. The praise names Vishnu, boon-giver to the Pandavas of the Kuru line, Hrishikesa, Uma's brother, dweller on northern Venkatam with bow and discus, as uncle, and Murugan as son of the destroyer of the triple city and kin of Kama, Subrahmanya of the six faces, at Thiruvanchiyam where the king grants release.
812.nuance: The confession is not the poet's own but a portrait of rulers, an argument from impermanence: ஒரு பிடி சாம்பல் பட்டது அறிகிலர். உன் அவாஞ்சை மிக்கு அடிதொழ நினையாரே may pun on the shrine's name (வாஞ்சியம், வாஞ்சை 'longing'). Murugan is called மைத்துனன் of Kama, both being in the poet's scheme Vishnu's kin.

links.note: Both use kings to show impermanence: the Naladiyar's commanders on elephants under the royal umbrella fall when their deeds turn, and 812's lords of elephant armies and conquered directions end as a handful of ash; 812 adds that they never thought to worship.

812 portrays kings who rule armies and swell with pride on cushions, until, among their kin, they are burnt to a handful of ash. Tirumanthiram 153 shows the land's lord mounting for the last time the burning-ground palanquin, people following and drums in front (காட்டுச் சிவிகையொன்று ஏறி). Both make the king the case of impermanence; Tirumular keeps the royal procession for the funeral, and the song adds the charge that they did not think to worship the feet.
